items.stem: Tariq took Jonas, an elderly neighbour who could not look after herself, into the family home and promised to care for her. Nadia did nothing to help when the danger arose, and Jonas was seriously harmed as a result. Discuss whether Tariq could be criminally liable for failing to act. Explain and apply the relevant law, using decided cases to support your advice.
items.answer: Law: there is no general duty to act in English law; a duty arises from contract (Pittwood), relationship (Gibbins and Proctor), voluntary assumption of care (Stone and Dobinson), creating danger (Miller) or public office (Dytham); the omission must cause the harm and be accompanied by the required mens rea. Application: Tariq took Jonas, an elderly neighbour who could not look after herself, into the family home and promised to care for her, so a duty arises from voluntary assumption of care (R v Stone and Dobinson (1977)); failing to act was a breach of that duty; causation and mens rea must then be proved for the particular offence. Conclusion: Tariq owed a duty to act based on voluntary assumption of care, so the failure to act can form the actus reus.

Conclusion [1]: Tariq owed a duty to act based on voluntary assumption of care, so the failure to act can form the actus reus Top band needs case authority used accurately and every relevant issue applied, not just described. items.stem: Mohammed was driving along a road in Mumbai when a swarm of bees flew in through the window and stung Mohammed repeatedly. Mohammed's car swerved and hit Yusuf, who was injured. Discuss whether Mohammed's conduct satisfies the actus reus requirement of an offence. Explain and apply the relevant law, using decided cases to support your advice. Comment on any uncertainty in the law.
items.answer: Law: the actus reus must be voluntary (Hill v Baxter 1958); involuntary movements caused by an external force are not acts of the defendant; a voluntary but careless act is still an act. Application: here a swarm of bees flew in through the window and stung Mohammed repeatedly; this movement was involuntary. Conclusion: If the movement was involuntary Mohammed has no actus reus; if voluntary, Mohammed may be liable; here it was involuntary.

items.stem: Lucas threatened to attack Isla in a car park in Toronto. To escape, Isla stopped to take selfies and then deliberately lay down in the road and was seriously injured. Discuss whether Lucas is the legal cause of Isla's injuries. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: factual causation: "but for" test; the victim's reaction does not break the chain if it is reasonably foreseeable (R v Roberts); only a "daft" reaction, out of proportion to the threat, breaks the chain (R v Williams 1992); the free, deliberate and informed act of the victim may break the chain (R v Kennedy (No 2)). Application: but for Lucas's conduct, Isla would not have been injured; Isla stopped to take selfies and then deliberately lay down in the road, which is a "daft" and unforeseeable reaction that may break the chain (R v Williams). Conclusion: Lucas is probably not liable for the injuries.

items.stem: Nadia stabbed Samuel during an argument in Lagos. Samuel was taken to hospital, where Samuel refused a blood transfusion because of religious beliefs. Samuel died. Discuss whether Nadia caused Samuel's death. Your answer should explain the relevant law, refer to decided cases and reach a reasoned conclusion.
items.answer: Law: factual causation: but for the defendant's act the result would not have occurred (R v White); legal causation: the act must be an operating and substantial cause (R v Smith); medical treatment breaks the chain only if so independent and potent (R v Cheshire), e.g. palpably wrong (R v Jordan); the thin skull rule applies (R v Blaue). Application: but for the stabbing Samuel would not have been in hospital, so factual causation is satisfied; here Samuel refused a blood transfusion because of religious beliefs, which raises the thin skull rule (R v Blaue); so Nadia is liable for the death. Conclusion: Nadia is liable for the death.

items.stem: Amara wanted to destroy evidence of a fraud. To do this, Amara set fire to the building at night. Ana, who was working late inside, was killed. Discuss whether Amara had the mens rea for murder. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: murder requires intention to kill or cause grievous bodily harm; direct intention: the result is the aim (R v Mohan); oblique intention: the jury may find intention if death or serious injury was a virtual certainty and the defendant appreciated this (R v Woollin; R v Nedrick); foresight is evidence of intention (R v Matthews and Alleyne). Application: Amara's aim was to destroy evidence of a fraud, not to kill, so there is no direct intention; death or serious injury was a virtual certainty as a result of the act; the jury is likely to find oblique intention if Amara appreciated this. Conclusion: The jury is likely to find that Amara had oblique intention for murder; otherwise manslaughter may be considered.

items.stem: Daniel hit Ana on the head with a brick during a fight in Riyadh. Believing Ana was dead, Daniel left Ana in a freezing field. In fact Ana was alive and died as a result of exposure. Discuss whether the actus reus and mens rea of murder coincide.
items.answer: Law: actus reus and mens rea must coincide; a series of acts can be one transaction (Thabo Meli v R); this applies without a preconceived plan (R v Church) and where the later act is an attempt to cover up (R v Le Brun). Application: when Daniel left Ana in a freezing field there was no mens rea, but the earlier blow was done with mens rea; the acts form one transaction, so they coincide. Conclusion: The actus reus and mens rea coincide across the series of acts, so Daniel can be liable for murder (or manslaughter if only intent for lesser harm).

items.stem: Diego runs a food factory in Manila. A piece of metal was found in a tin of soup. Diego had no idea anything had gone wrong. Diego is charged with an offence under the (fictional) Food Safety Act 2015, which does not mention any mental element. Discuss whether Diego is likely to be liable even though Diego was not at fault. Explain the relevant legal rules before applying them.
items.answer: Law: presumption of mens rea for statutory offences (Sweet v Parsley 1970; B v DPP 2000); Gammon (1985): presumption displaced for regulatory offences of social concern where strict liability promotes observance; examples: Smedleys v Breed (food), Alphacell v Woodward (pollution), Harrow LBC v Shah (sales to minors); some statutes provide a due diligence defence. Application: the Food Safety Act 2015 is silent on mens rea, so the presumption applies at first; the offence concerns public safety and is regulatory, so the presumption is likely to be displaced; that Diego had no idea anything had gone wrong would not help unless there is a due diligence defence. Conclusion: The offence is likely to be strict liability, so Diego is probably liable despite not being at fault.

items.answer: The physical element of a crime: a voluntary act, omission or state of affairs, together with any required circumstances and consequences.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: basic/partial definition; 2 marks: full and accurate definition, i.e. the physical element of a crime: a voluntary act, omission or state of affairs, together with any required circumstances and consequences. [2]

items.stem: Explain why the actus reus of a crime must be voluntary.
items.answer: Criminal liability is based on choice: it would be unjust to punish someone for movements they could not control, such as reflexes or acts during a seizure (Hill v Baxter).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: idea of control/choice; 1 mark: example or case. [2]

items.stem: Leila was driving along a road in Singapore when Leila looked down to read a text message. Leila's car swerved and hit Ines, who was injured. State, with a brief reason, the most likely legal outcome.
items.answer: If the movement was involuntary Leila has no actus reus; if voluntary, Leila may be liable; here it was voluntary. Reason: the actus reus must be voluntary (Hill v Baxter 1958)
items.markingKey: 1 mark: correct outcome (if the movement was involuntary Leila has no actus reus; if voluntary, Leila may be liable; here it was voluntary). 1 mark: reason based on the rule, e.g. the actus reus must be voluntary (Hill v Baxter 1958). [2]

items.stem: Amara was driving along a road in Colombo when a swarm of bees flew in through the window and stung Amara repeatedly. Amara's car swerved and hit Sofia, who was injured. Discuss whether Amara's conduct satisfies the actus reus requirement of an offence.
items.answer: Law: the actus reus must be voluntary (Hill v Baxter 1958); involuntary movements caused by an external force are not acts of the defendant; a voluntary but careless act is still an act. Application: here a swarm of bees flew in through the window and stung Amara repeatedly; this movement was involuntary. Conclusion: If the movement was involuntary Amara has no actus reus; if voluntary, Amara may be liable; here it was involuntary.

items.stem: State what is meant by 'factual causation'.
items.answer: The "but for" test: the defendant's conduct is a factual cause of the result if the result would not have happened but for that conduct (R v White).

items.stem: Sofia chased with a knife Arjun in a car park in Kathmandu. To escape, Arjun jumped from a first-floor balcony and was seriously injured. Discuss whether Sofia is the legal cause of Arjun's injuries. Consider all the relevant issues and reach a justified conclusion.
items.answer: Law: factual causation: "but for" test; the victim's reaction does not break the chain if it is reasonably foreseeable (R v Roberts); only a "daft" reaction, out of proportion to the threat, breaks the chain (R v Williams 1992); the free, deliberate and informed act of the victim may break the chain (R v Kennedy (No 2)). Application: but for Sofia's conduct, Arjun would not have been injured; Arjun jumped from a first-floor balcony, which is a foreseeable reaction unless "daft" (R v Williams). Conclusion: Sofia is probably liable for the injuries.

items.stem: Leila runs a chemical plant in Singapore. A sealed tank cracked and polluted a nearby river. Leila had trained staff carefully and carried out regular checks. Leila is charged with an offence under the (fictional) River Protection Act 2017, which does not mention any mental element. Discuss whether Leila is likely to be liable even though Leila was not at fault. Refer to at least one decided case.
items.answer: Law: presumption of mens rea for statutory offences (Sweet v Parsley 1970; B v DPP 2000); Gammon (1985): presumption displaced for regulatory offences of social concern where strict liability promotes observance; examples: Smedleys v Breed (food), Alphacell v Woodward (pollution), Harrow LBC v Shah (sales to minors); some statutes provide a due diligence defence. Application: the River Protection Act 2017 is silent on mens rea, so the presumption applies at first; the offence concerns public safety and is regulatory, so the presumption is likely to be displaced; that Leila had trained staff carefully and carried out regular checks would not help unless there is a due diligence defence. Conclusion: The offence is likely to be strict liability, so Leila is probably liable despite not being at fault.

items.stem: Using your knowledge of the law, evaluate the law on liability for omissions.
items.answer: For: respects individual autonomy; duties are recognised in clear situations; avoids imposing heavy burdens on bystanders. Against: moral obligation to help strangers is ignored; the categories are uncertain (Stone and Dobinson); distinction between acts and omissions can be artificial (Bland); other countries (e.g. France) impose a duty to rescue. Conclusion: The law strikes a defensible balance, though the categories of duty are not always clear.

items.stem: Evaluate the rules on intervening acts in causation.

items.answer: Law: presumption of mens rea for statutory offences (Sweet v Parsley 1970; B v DPP 2000); Gammon (1985): presumption displaced for regulatory offences of social concern where strict liability promotes observance; examples: Smedleys v Breed (food), Alphacell v Woodward (pollution), Harrow LBC v Shah (sales to minors); some statutes provide a due diligence defence. Application: the Food Safety Act 2015 is silent on mens rea, so the presumption applies at first; the offence concerns public safety and is regulatory, so the presumption is likely to be displaced; that Chloe had trained staff carefully and carried out regular checks would not help unless there is a due diligence defence. Conclusion: The offence is likely to be strict liability, so Chloe is probably liable despite not being at fault.
